tool.name: Snowflake
tool.tagline: Cloud data warehouse with separate storage and elastic compute
tool.description: Snowflake is a fully managed cloud data platform that stores data once and lets any number of independent virtual warehouses query it with standard SQL. Data teams use it for analytics, ELT pipelines, semi-structured data and data sharing between organizations. Learning it means learning how warehouses, micro-partitions and roles drive cost, speed and security.

glossary.def: A database built for analysing large amounts of history (sales, clicks, readings) with big read-only queries, rather than for many small updates.
A cloud data warehouse sold as a service, which keeps storage and compute (virtual warehouses) separate so each can grow and be billed on its own.
Your organisation's own Snowflake space, in one cloud and region, holding its users, roles, warehouses and databases.
One of the files Snowflake stores a table in: about 50 to 500 MB of rows, kept column by column and never edited, with min/max values recorded for each column.
In Snowflake: a named group of computers that runs queries. It holds no data, starts and stops on demand and is billed in credits while running.
Snowflake's billing unit for compute: an X-Small warehouse uses 1 credit per hour, and each size up doubles it.
Snowflake's website, with SQL worksheets, dashboards, query history and administration pages.
In Snowflake: anything you create and name, such as a table, view, stage or warehouse. (A JSON object, by contrast, is a set of named values in curly braces.)
A cheaper Snowflake table kind with at most 1 day of Time Travel and no Fail-safe; temporary tables also vanish when the session ends.
A further 7 days after Time Travel during which only Snowflake Support can recover a permanent table's data.
In Snowflake: a named place where files wait to be loaded or after being unloaded, either managed by Snowflake (internal) or in your own cloud storage (external).
In Snowflake: a saved description of files to load (CSV with a header, JSON, Parquet...) that COPY INTO and stages can reuse.
Snowflake's column type that can hold any JSON value (object, array, text, number...), queried with paths like col:customer.name.
A Snowflake table function that turns each element of an array, or each key of an object, into its own row.
Snowflake's ability to query or restore a table as it was at a past moment, within its retention period (1 day by default, up to 90).
Making a copy of a Snowflake table, schema or database that shares the original's files, so it's instant and costs no storage until either side changes.
In Snowflake: a role granted to another role passes all its privileges up, so the receiving role can do everything the granted one can.
A Snowflake grant on objects that don't exist yet, such as all future tables in a schema, so new tables get the privilege automatically.
Skipping files that can't contain matching rows, using their recorded min/max values, before reading any data.
In Snowflake: arranging a table's rows so similar values of chosen columns sit in the same micro-partitions, which makes pruning work.
The columns or expressions a Snowflake table is told to keep its data arranged by (CLUSTER BY), maintained in the background for credits.
Snowsight's diagram of how a query ran: each step, its time, and how many micro-partitions it scanned out of the total.
In Snowflake: an object that records the changes (inserts, updates, deletes) made to a table since the stream was last read by a committed change.
In Snowflake: a saved SQL statement that runs on a schedule or after another task, created suspended until you resume it.
Snowflake's service for loading files automatically as soon as they arrive in a stage (Snowpipe Streaming sends rows directly).
A Snowflake table defined by a query and a target lag; Snowflake refreshes it automatically, only processing changes when it can.
How out of date a dynamic table may be compared with its sources, which Snowflake schedules refreshes to meet.
Snowflake's library for Python, Java and Scala that builds queries as chains of method calls (DataFrames) and runs them as SQL inside Snowflake.
A table-like object in code (pandas, Snowpark) with rows and named columns that you filter, group and join with method calls.
A Snowflake warehouse that adds and removes extra clusters automatically when queries start waiting, to run more queries at once.
A Snowflake limit on credits per warehouse or account per period that can warn and suspend warehouses when reached.
A Snowflake service that builds an index-like lookup structure so queries matching very few rows skip most micro-partitions.
A Snowflake rule attached to columns that shows the real value or a hidden version (like ***) depending on who is querying.
A Snowflake view whose definition is hidden and which can't be tricked into revealing filtered rows; required for sharing views.
In Snowflake: an object that gives other Snowflake accounts live, read-only access to chosen data without copying it.

concepts.name: Snowflake's architecture
concepts.summary: Storage, compute (virtual warehouses) and cloud services are separate layers that grow and are billed independently.
concepts.why: Every cost and performance decision in Snowflake follows from this separation.
concepts.body:
A normal database such as PostgreSQL runs as one server program on one computer, which holds both the data and the processing power that answers queries. For analysing very large amounts of history, the job of a **data warehouse**, that becomes a limit: a bigger workload needs a bigger computer, and everyone's queries compete for it. **Snowflake** is a data warehouse sold as a service that splits those jobs apart.

It runs in the **cloud**: on computers rented from Amazon (AWS), Microsoft (Azure) or Google, which you never see. You pick one when you create your Snowflake **account**, your organisation's own Snowflake space. Snowflake then has three layers that grow and are billed separately:

- **Storage**: tables are kept in the cloud provider's file storage, squeezed to take less space (**compression**), in **columnar** form: each column is stored on its own, so a query reads only the columns it needs. The files are never edited in place; a change writes new ones. Snowflake calls them **micro-partitions**. You pay per **terabyte** (about a trillion bytes) stored per month and never manage files yourself.
- **Compute**: **virtual warehouses** run your queries. Despite the name, a warehouse holds no data: it is a group of rented computers working together (a **cluster**) that reads tables when needed. Any number of warehouses can read the same tables at once without competing. You pay in **credits**, Snowflake's billing unit, only while a warehouse runs.
- **Cloud services**: the brain that handles logins, the bookkeeping of which files make up each table (**metadata**), planning each query, transactions and access control. It is usually free; you are charged only when its daily use exceeds 10% of your warehouse compute.

Two consequences matter every day. First, you keep workloads apart by giving them separate warehouses: the nightly job that loads and reshapes data and the morning dashboards never slow each other down. Second, storage is cheap and compute is what costs money, so performance work is mostly about reading less data in less warehouse time.

You work with Snowflake through **Snowsight**, its website with SQL worksheets; through command-line tools (Snowflake CLI, SnowSQL) typed into a terminal; through connectors that let programs in Python, Java and other languages send queries; and through tools such as dbt. All of them send SQL. Snowflake's dialect is standard SQL with extensions.
concepts.code:
-- Which warehouse, role, database and schema is this session using?
SELECT CURRENT_WAREHOUSE(), CURRENT_ROLE(), CURRENT_DATABASE(), CURRENT_SCHEMA();

-- Snowflake ships a shared sample database you can query right away
SELECT c_mktsegment, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF1.CUSTOMER
GROUP BY c_mktsegment
ORDER BY customers DESC;
-- BUILDING    30142
-- FURNITURE   29968
-- ...
takeaways: Storage, compute and cloud services grow and are billed separately
Warehouses are compute only; many can query the same data at once
Compute time, not storage, is usually the main cost
pitfalls: Thinking a warehouse is where data is stored; it only runs queries.

quiz.q: Two teams run heavy queries on the same table at the same time from different warehouses. What happens?
options: Both run without competing for compute
The second query waits for a table lock
The data is copied to each warehouse first
quiz.explain: Warehouses are independent compute clusters reading shared storage, so they don't contend.

concepts.name: Virtual warehouses and credits
concepts.summary: Create and size warehouses, use auto-suspend and auto-resume, and understand per-second credit billing.
concepts.why: Warehouse settings are the main lever on your Snowflake bill.
concepts.body:
A **virtual warehouse** is a named compute cluster. Sizes go X-Small, Small, Medium, Large, X-Large and up to 6X-Large; each step doubles both the compute and the credits per hour (X-Small uses 1 credit per hour, Small 2, Medium 4, and so on).

Billing is **per second**, with a 60-second minimum each time a warehouse starts. Two settings keep that cheap:

- `AUTO_SUSPEND = 60` suspends the warehouse after 60 idle seconds. Suspended warehouses cost nothing.
- `AUTO_RESUME = TRUE` starts it automatically when a query arrives, usually within a second or two.

Choosing a size: a bigger warehouse makes a single large query faster, roughly in proportion for scan-heavy work, so doubling the size for half the running time costs the same credits. It does not help many small queries waiting their turn in a line (a **queue**). Running many queries at the same time is called **concurrency**, and it is solved by multi-cluster warehouses (several clusters behind one warehouse name) or by separate warehouses per workload. Start small, check query times and waiting in the query history, and resize with `ALTER WAREHOUSE` at any time; running queries finish on the old size.

A warehouse also keeps a local **cache**: a copy, kept close by, of data it has recently read, so reading it again is faster. Suspending it drops that cache, so very short auto-suspend times can make dashboards (pages of charts that rerun queries) slower. Values between 60 seconds and a few minutes are typical.
takeaways: Each size step doubles compute and credits per hour
Per-second billing with a 60-second minimum per resume
Always set AUTO_SUSPEND and AUTO_RESUME
Bigger size speeds big queries; more clusters help concurrency
pitfalls: Leaving a warehouse running with a long or no auto-suspend, burning credits while idle.

quiz.q: A query takes 20 minutes on a Medium warehouse and scans a lot of data. Roughly what happens on a Large?
options: About 5 minutes for half the credits
About 10 minutes for about the same credits
It fails because size can't change
quiz.explain: Large has twice the compute at twice the rate; for scan-heavy queries runtime roughly halves, so cost stays similar.

quiz.q: Many small dashboard queries are queuing. What usually helps most?
options: More clusters (multi-cluster) or a separate warehouse
quiz.explain: Queuing is a concurrency problem; more clusters run more queries in parallel.

concepts.name: Databases, schemas and context
concepts.summary: Navigate the account → database → schema → object hierarchy, set your session's context with USE, and know how names change case.
concepts.why: Every query depends on the right context and fully qualified names, and identifier case trips up everyone once.
concepts.body:
Objects in Snowflake live in a hierarchy: an **account** contains **databases**, a database contains **schemas**, and a schema contains tables, views, functions, procedures and other kinds that later lessons introduce; Snowflake calls all of these **objects**. Warehouses, users and roles are account-level objects.

A fully qualified name is `database.schema.object`, e.g. `SALES.PUBLIC.ORDERS`. Your connection to Snowflake, from logging in until you disconnect, is a **session**. Names without a database and schema are looked up in the session's current database and schema, which you set with `USE DATABASE`, `USE SCHEMA` or both at once (`USE SCHEMA sales.public`). The session also has a current role and current warehouse, and a query needs all of them: a role with privileges and a running warehouse.

**Identifiers**: unquoted names are stored and resolved in **upper case**, so `orders`, `Orders` and `ORDERS` are the same table. Double quotes make a name case-sensitive: `"orders"` is a different table from `orders`. Tools that put quotes around every name (some loading tools and code libraries) can therefore create lowercase tables you then have to quote forever. Stick to unquoted names.

Useful commands: `SHOW DATABASES`, `SHOW SCHEMAS`, `SHOW TABLES IN SCHEMA x`, `DESCRIBE TABLE t`, and `GET_DDL('TABLE', 't')` to see the DDL of any object. `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` views in each database answer the same questions in SQL.
takeaways: Hierarchy: account → database → schema → objects
A query needs context: role, warehouse, database and schema
Unquoted identifiers are upper-cased; quoted ones are case-sensitive
pitfalls: Creating objects with quoted lowercase names and then failing to find them unquoted.

quiz.q: A table was created as "events" (with quotes). Which query finds it?
quiz.explain: Quoted identifiers keep their case; unquoted events resolves to EVENTS, a different name.

concepts.name: Tables and data types
concepts.summary: Create permanent, transient and temporary tables with Snowflake types like NUMBER, VARCHAR, TIMESTAMP_NTZ/LTZ/TZ and VARIANT.
concepts.why: Types and table kinds affect correctness, time-zone behaviour and how much storage protection you pay for.
concepts.body:
Snowflake's types are mostly familiar, with a few specifics:

- `NUMBER(p, s)` is the core numeric type; `INT` and `BIGINT` are aliases for `NUMBER(38, 0)`. `FLOAT` holds approximate (floating-point) numbers.
- `VARCHAR` with no length is fine. The declared length doesn't change storage, so there's no reason to write `VARCHAR(255)`.
- Timestamps come in three flavours. `TIMESTAMP_NTZ` is wall-clock time with no zone, `TIMESTAMP_LTZ` is an exact moment, shown in the session's time zone, and `TIMESTAMP_TZ` stores an offset with each value. Plain `TIMESTAMP` maps to NTZ by default. Pick deliberately; for event times, LTZ or TZ avoids ambiguity.
- `VARIANT`, `OBJECT` and `ARRAY` hold data whose shape varies from row to row, such as **JSON** (text documents of named values and lists; see the VARIANT lesson).
- `BOOLEAN`, `DATE`, `TIME`, `BINARY`, `GEOGRAPHY` and `VECTOR` also exist.

**Constraints**: `PRIMARY KEY`, `UNIQUE` and `FOREIGN KEY` can be declared on standard tables but are **not enforced**; only `NOT NULL` is. They serve as documentation and hints for tools.

Table kinds trade safety for cost. **Permanent** tables (the default) have Time Travel and a 7-day Fail-safe. **Transient** tables have at most 1 day of Time Travel and no Fail-safe, which suits staging data you can reload. **Temporary** tables live only for the session. `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` (CTAS) and `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE` are everyday idioms.
takeaways: INT is NUMBER(38,0); VARCHAR length doesn't affect storage
Choose TIMESTAMP_NTZ, LTZ or TZ deliberately
Only NOT NULL is enforced; PK/UNIQUE/FK are informational
Transient tables skip Fail-safe and cost less to keep
pitfalls: Relying on a PRIMARY KEY to prevent duplicate rows; remove duplicates while loading instead.

quiz.q: You insert two rows with the same id into a table declared with id INT PRIMARY KEY. What happens?
options: The second row replaces the first
quiz.explain: Snowflake does not enforce primary keys on standard tables.

quiz.q: Which table type is best for a staging table rebuilt every night from files?
quiz.explain: Transient tables avoid Fail-safe storage costs, and the data can simply be reloaded.

concepts.name: Stages and COPY INTO
concepts.summary: Load files in bulk: put them in a stage, describe them with a file format object, and load them with COPY INTO.
concepts.why: COPY INTO is the standard way data gets into Snowflake, and its load history prevents duplicate loads.
concepts.body:
Bulk loading has three pieces.

**Stages** are locations of files. There are internal stages managed by Snowflake: the user stage `@~`, a table stage `@%orders`, and named stages `CREATE STAGE my_stage`. There are also **external stages**, which point at your own file storage in Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure, usually through a storage integration (a saved, trusted connection) so no passwords or keys are written into SQL. Upload files from your computer to an internal stage with `PUT file://... @stage`, run from SnowSQL or the Snowflake CLI, or with the upload dialog in Snowsight.

A **file format** object describes the files: `TYPE = CSV` with options such as `SKIP_HEADER`, `FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BY`, `NULL_IF`, or `TYPE = JSON | PARQUET | AVRO | ORC | XML`. Save a format as a named object and reuse it.

**COPY INTO table FROM @stage** loads many files at the same time on your warehouse. Important behaviour:

- Snowflake remembers which files it loaded into each table for 64 days and **skips them** on later runs, so rerunning a COPY is safe. `FORCE = TRUE` loads them again anyway.
- `ON_ERROR` defaults to `ABORT_STATEMENT`; `CONTINUE` or `SKIP_FILE` tolerate bad rows or files.
- `VALIDATION_MODE = RETURN_ERRORS` tests the load without loading anything and reports problems.
- For Parquet and other column-based file types, `MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME = CASE_INSENSITIVE` maps columns by name.

Files of roughly 100 to 250 MB (**megabytes**, millions of bytes) after compression load fastest, because each file is handled by one worker inside the warehouse, and many medium files keep all of them busy.
takeaways: Stage (where files are) + file format (what they are) + COPY INTO (load)
COPY skips files already loaded into that table within 64 days
Use VALIDATION_MODE to test and ON_ERROR to control failures
pitfalls: Using FORCE = TRUE to 'retry' a load and ending up with duplicated rows.

quiz.q: You rerun the same COPY INTO over a stage path where every file was loaded yesterday. What happens?
options: COPY fails with a duplicate error
The files are skipped thanks to load metadata
quiz.explain: Snowflake tracks loaded files per table and skips them unless FORCE = TRUE.

concepts.name: VARIANT and querying JSON
concepts.summary: Store JSON in VARIANT columns and query it with colon and dot paths, bracket access and :: casts.
concepts.why: Event data and messages from other systems arrive as JSON, and Snowflake lets you query it directly without a fixed schema.
concepts.body:
A **VARIANT** column can hold any JSON value: an object (named values in curly braces), an array (a list in square brackets), a string, number, boolean or null. Load JSON files with `COPY INTO` using `TYPE = JSON`, or convert text with `PARSE_JSON('...')`. Snowflake stores VARIANT data in a columnar way internally, extracting common paths into their own columns, so queries on frequent keys are efficient.

Writing paths:

- `src:customer` reads the top-level key `customer` (the colon is only for the first level).
- `src:customer.address.city` walks nested objects with dots.
- `src:items[0]` picks array elements, counting from 0, and `src['odd key']` handles names with spaces or special characters.
- Key names in paths are **case-sensitive**, unlike SQL identifiers.

Values extracted from a VARIANT are still VARIANT. Selected strings display with double quotes, and comparisons may not behave as you expect. **Cast** them with `::`, as in `src:customer.name::STRING`, `src:total::NUMBER(10,2)`, `src:ts::TIMESTAMP_TZ`. Use `TRY_CAST` or the `TRY_TO_*` functions to get NULL instead of an error for bad values.

Missing paths return SQL NULL, while a JSON `null` value is a VARIANT null that displays as `null`; `IS_NULL_VALUE()` tells them apart. Building JSON goes the other way: `OBJECT_CONSTRUCT('id', id, 'total', total)`, `ARRAY_CONSTRUCT`, `ARRAY_AGG` and `OBJECT_AGG`. `TYPEOF(v)` shows what a value holds.
takeaways: col:key.nested[0] navigates JSON; key names are case-sensitive
Cast extracted values with :: (or TRY_CAST) before comparing or aggregating
OBJECT_CONSTRUCT and ARRAY_AGG build JSON back up
pitfalls: Comparing or joining on uncast VARIANT values and getting no matches or odd sorting.

quiz.q: What does SELECT src:Name return if the JSON key is spelled "name"?
quiz.explain: JSON path elements are case-sensitive, so a mismatched key is simply missing.

quiz.q: Why write src:total::NUMBER(10,2) instead of src:total?
options: To make the query run on a smaller warehouse
To turn the VARIANT into a typed value for math, comparison and correct sorting
Because :: is required by COPY INTO
quiz.explain: Extracted values stay VARIANT until cast.

concepts.name: FLATTEN: arrays and nested data to rows
concepts.summary: Explode arrays and objects into rows with LATERAL FLATTEN, keep empty arrays with OUTER, and flatten every nested level.
concepts.why: Line items, tags and nested events must become rows before you can join or aggregate them.
concepts.body:
`FLATTEN` is a table function that turns each element of an array (or each key of an object) into a row. You combine it with the source table through `LATERAL`, or the equivalent `, TABLE(FLATTEN(...))` form, so each row is joined to its own elements.

Each output row has columns you refer to through the alias:

- `VALUE`: the element itself (a VARIANT, so cast it);
- `INDEX`: the position in an array, `KEY`: the key for objects;
- `PATH`, `SEQ` (identifies the source row) and `THIS` (the element being flattened).

Options:

- `OUTER => TRUE` emits one row with NULLs for empty or missing arrays. Without it, source rows whose array is empty **disappear**, just like an inner join.
- `RECURSIVE => TRUE` walks every nested level, which is useful for discovering a document's keys.
- `PATH => 'a.b'` flattens a nested path.

To flatten two levels, such as orders → items → discounts, chain two LATERAL FLATTENs, the second taking `f1.value:discounts`. Going the other direction, `ARRAY_AGG(... ) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...)` re-nests rows into an array.

A common pattern is a view or dbt model that flattens raw VARIANT events into typed, relational columns once, so analysts query normal tables.
concepts.code:
-- raw_events.src = {"id": 7, "items": [{"sku":"A1","qty":2},{"sku":"B9","qty":1}], ...}
SELECT e.src:id::INT        AS order_id,
       i.index              AS line_no,
       i.value:sku::STRING  AS sku,
       i.value:qty::INT     AS qty
FROM raw_events e,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.src:items) i;
-- 7 | 0 | A1 | 2
-- 7 | 1 | B9 | 1

-- Keep orders with no items
SELECT e.src:id::INT AS order_id, i.value:sku::STRING AS sku
FROM raw_events e,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.src:items, OUTER => TRUE) i;

-- Discover every key path in the documents
SELECT DISTINCT f.path
FROM raw_events e, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.src, RECURSIVE => TRUE) f;
takeaways: LATERAL FLATTEN turns array elements into rows: use value, index, key
Without OUTER => TRUE, rows with empty arrays vanish
RECURSIVE => TRUE lists every nested path
pitfalls: Counting orders after flattening without OUTER and silently losing orders with no items.

quiz.q: An order has "items": []. Using LATERAL FLATTEN(input => src:items) without OUTER, how many rows does that order produce?
options: One row per key of the order
quiz.explain: An empty array produces no elements, so the order disappears unless OUTER => TRUE.

concepts.name: Time Travel, UNDROP and zero-copy cloning
concepts.summary: Query past versions of data with AT/BEFORE, restore dropped objects with UNDROP, and clone databases instantly without copying data.
concepts.why: Recovering from a bad UPDATE or spinning up a full dev copy takes seconds once you know these features.
concepts.body:
Because micro-partitions are never changed once written, Snowflake can keep old versions of a table around. **Time Travel** lets you query or restore data as it was within the retention period: 1 day by default, up to 90 days for permanent objects on Enterprise edition (`DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS`). Transient and temporary tables allow at most 1 day.

- `SELECT ... FROM t AT(TIMESTAMP => '2025-06-01 09:00'::TIMESTAMP_LTZ)`
- `AT(OFFSET => -60*30)`: 30 minutes ago, in seconds.
- `BEFORE(STATEMENT => '<query id>')`: just before a specific statement ran, ideal after a bad `DELETE`.
- `UNDROP TABLE | SCHEMA | DATABASE` restores a dropped object.

After Time Travel ends, permanent tables enter a 7-day **Fail-safe** that only Snowflake Support can recover from. Both periods consume storage for changed data.

**Zero-copy cloning** creates a new table, schema or whole database that initially shares the original's micro-partitions: `CREATE DATABASE dev CLONE prod`. It completes in seconds or minutes regardless of size and costs no storage until either side changes data. Clones can be combined with Time Travel, `CLONE t AT(...)`, to capture one moment in time.

A common recovery move: clone the table as it was before the bad statement, check it, then swap it in with `ALTER TABLE ... SWAP WITH ...`.
takeaways: AT / BEFORE query past data within the retention period
UNDROP restores dropped tables, schemas and databases
Clones share micro-partitions: instant and free until data diverges
pitfalls: Assuming Time Travel is a backup with unlimited history; it lasts only the retention period.

quiz.q: What does CREATE DATABASE dev CLONE prod cost in storage immediately after it runs?
options: Almost nothing; storage grows only as either database changes
It depends on the warehouse size
quiz.explain: Clones reference the same immutable micro-partitions until changes create new ones.

concepts.name: Roles and access control
concepts.summary: Grant privileges to roles, not users; build role hierarchies; and understand system roles, ownership and future grants.
concepts.why: Every query runs under a role, and a clean role design is what keeps a Snowflake account secure and manageable.
concepts.body:
Snowflake uses **role-based access control (RBAC)**: permissions go to roles, and people get roles. Privileges (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `USAGE`, `CREATE TABLE`, `OPERATE`...) are granted to **roles**, roles are granted to users, and roles can be granted to other roles, forming a hierarchy in which a parent **inherits** its children's privileges: it can do everything they can. A session has a current role (`USE ROLE`), plus optional secondary roles.

System roles to know:

- `ACCOUNTADMIN`: top-level; use sparingly, never as a daily role.
- `SECURITYADMIN` manages grants, `USERADMIN` creates users and roles.
- `SYSADMIN` creates warehouses and databases; custom roles should be granted to it so admins can see what they create.
- `PUBLIC`: granted to everyone.

Reading a table needs a **chain** of privileges: `USAGE` on the database, `USAGE` on the schema, `SELECT` on the table, and `USAGE` on a warehouse to run the query. A missing link produces "does not exist or not authorized", which is deliberately vague.

Every object has an **owner** role (the role that created it) with full control. **Future grants** (`GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA ...`) apply to objects created later, which avoids granting again after every release.

A common design is two layers: **access roles** holding privileges on objects (e.g. `SALES_READ`) and **functional roles** matching jobs (e.g. `ANALYST`) that are granted the access roles they need.
takeaways: Privileges go to roles; roles go to users and other roles
Reading needs USAGE on database, schema and warehouse plus SELECT
Future grants cover tables created later
Keep ACCOUNTADMIN for rare admin work
pitfalls: Granting SELECT on a table but forgetting USAGE on its database or schema.

quiz.q: A role has SELECT on shop.raw.orders but queries fail with 'does not exist or not authorized'. What is the most likely missing privilege?
options: USAGE on the database or schema
quiz.explain: Access requires USAGE on every container in the path, not just SELECT on the table.

quiz.q: Why grant custom roles to SYSADMIN?
options: So SYSADMIN inherits their privileges and can manage the objects they own
quiz.explain: Connecting custom roles to the hierarchy keeps their objects visible to administrators.

concepts.name: Snowflake SQL extensions: QUALIFY and friends
concepts.summary: Write tighter queries with QUALIFY, GROUP BY ALL, SELECT * EXCLUDE, IFF, ILIKE, MIN_BY/MAX_BY and the :: cast.
concepts.why: These extensions remove whole subqueries from everyday analytics SQL.
concepts.body:
Snowflake SQL is ANSI-compatible with handy additions.

- **QUALIFY** filters on window functions the way `HAVING` filters on aggregates, so "latest row per key" needs no subquery: `QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1`.
- **GROUP BY ALL** groups by every non-aggregate expression in the select list.
- **SELECT * EXCLUDE (col1, col2)** and **SELECT * RENAME (a AS b)** avoid spelling out wide column lists. `REPLACE` is also available.
- **IFF(cond, a, b)** is a compact two-branch CASE; `NVL`, `ZEROIFNULL`, `NULLIFZERO` and `EQUAL_NULL` handle NULLs.
- **ILIKE** is case-insensitive LIKE; `LIKE ANY ('a%', 'b%')` matches a list of patterns.
- **MIN_BY(x, y)** / **MAX_BY(x, y)** return x from the row with the min or max y.
- `expr::type` is shorthand for `CAST`; `TRY_CAST` and `TRY_TO_NUMBER` return NULL instead of failing.
- Column aliases can be reused later in the same select list and in `WHERE`.
- `SAMPLE (10)` reads a random 10% of rows, and `RESULT_SCAN(LAST_QUERY_ID())` lets you query the previous result.

Date helpers worth knowing: `DATE_TRUNC('month', ts)`, `DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_DATE())` and `DATEDIFF(day, a, b)`.
concepts.code:
-- Latest status per order, no subquery needed
SELECT order_id, status, updated_at,
       IFF(status = 'shipped', 'done', 'open') AS state
FROM order_events
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1;

SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at)        AS month,
       region,
       COUNT(*)                              AS n_orders,
       COUNT_IF(status ILIKE 'cancel%')      AS cancelled,
       ROUND(cancelled / n_orders, 3)        AS cancel_rate,    -- reuses aliases
       MAX_BY(order_id, amount)              AS biggest_order
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= DATEADD(month, -6, CURRENT_DATE())
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY month, region;

SELECT * EXCLUDE (internal_notes, raw_payload) FROM customers LIMIT 10;
takeaways: QUALIFY filters window-function results directly
GROUP BY ALL and SELECT * EXCLUDE cut repetitive typing
MAX_BY / MIN_BY, IFF, ILIKE and :: are daily shortcuts
pitfalls: Writing QUALIFY in a dialect that lacks it when porting SQL elsewhere, e.g. to PostgreSQL.

quiz.q: Which clause keeps only the first row per customer by a window function without a subquery?
quiz.explain: QUALIFY is evaluated after window functions, so it can filter on them.

concepts.name: Result cache and warehouse cache
concepts.summary: Understand the saved result cache, the warehouse's local cache and answers from metadata alone, and when each applies.
concepts.why: Caches explain why the same query is sometimes instant and free, and sometimes not.
concepts.body:
Snowflake has three layers that can make a query fast or free.

**Result cache** (cloud services layer): when a query is repeated, its result is returned instantly **without using a warehouse**, if

- the query text is identical (same capitals and spacing),
- the underlying data has not changed,
- it contains no functions whose result changes from run to run, such as `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()` or `RANDOM()`,
- and the role has the necessary privileges.

Results are kept for 24 hours, and each reuse extends that, up to 31 days. Set `USE_CACHED_RESULT = FALSE` in your session when timing queries.

**Warehouse cache** (local SSD): a running warehouse caches the micro-partitions it has read. Later queries reading the same data on the same warehouse skip remote storage reads. It is lost when the warehouse suspends or resizes, which is one reason to group similar workloads on one warehouse and avoid ultra-short auto-suspend for dashboards.

**Metadata**: Snowflake keeps row counts and min/max values per micro-partition, so `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t` or `MAX(id)` on a whole table can be answered from metadata alone, with no warehouse running.

The query profile shows which applied: "QUERY RESULT REUSE" for the result cache, and a "percentage scanned from cache" figure for the warehouse cache.
takeaways: Result cache: identical query + unchanged data = instant, no warehouse
Warehouse cache lives on local SSD and is lost on suspend
COUNT/MIN/MAX on whole tables come from metadata
pitfalls: Timing a warehouse size with the result cache on, and measuring cached answers instead of real work.

quiz.q: Which change would prevent a repeated query from using the result cache?
options: Running it from a different warehouse
Adding CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() to the select list
Running it two hours later with no data changes
quiz.explain: Non-deterministic functions make results ineligible; the warehouse used doesn't matter.

concepts.name: Micro-partitions, pruning and clustering
concepts.summary: See how micro-partition metadata enables pruning, read the query profile, and decide when a clustering key is worth it.
concepts.why: Pruning is the main reason Snowflake queries are fast or slow on large tables.
concepts.body:
Every table is stored as **micro-partitions**: files that are never edited, holding about 50 to 500 MB of uncompressed data each, stored column by column. For each micro-partition and column Snowflake keeps metadata such as min and max values, distinct counts and null counts.

When a query filters (`WHERE event_date = '2025-06-01'`), the optimizer compares the filter to that metadata and **prunes** micro-partitions that cannot contain matches, before reading anything. In the **query profile**, the TableScan node shows "Partitions scanned" versus "Partitions total"; that ratio is the first thing to check on a slow query.

Pruning works only if matching values are concentrated in few micro-partitions. Data loaded in time order is naturally well clustered by time. Data that arrives randomly, or a filter on a column unrelated to load order, spreads values across every micro-partition.

A **clustering key** (`ALTER TABLE t CLUSTER BY (event_date, tenant_id)`) tells Snowflake to reorganize data in the background (Automatic Clustering) so similar values sit together. Consider it when:

- the table is large (multi-terabyte, or many thousands of micro-partitions),
- queries filter on the same columns most of the time and prune poorly,
- the table isn't rewritten constantly, since churn makes reclustering expensive.

Automatic Clustering consumes credits. Measure with `SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION`, where a lower `average_depth` is better. Use low-to-medium-cardinality columns or expressions like `TO_DATE(ts)` rather than raw timestamps or ids.
takeaways: Micro-partition min/max metadata lets Snowflake prune before reading
Check partitions scanned vs total in the query profile
Clustering keys pay off on large, frequently filtered, rarely rewritten tables
pitfalls: Clustering by a high-cardinality column such as a raw timestamp or a random ID, which is costly to maintain and prunes little.

quiz.q: A query on a 30 TB table scans 47,000 of 48,000 partitions despite a selective date filter. What is the likely cause?
options: The table has no primary key
Rows for each date are spread across almost all micro-partitions
quiz.explain: Poor clustering on the filter column means min/max ranges overlap the filter everywhere, so little is pruned.

concepts.name: Streams, tasks and Snowpipe
concepts.summary: Track changes with streams, apply them on a schedule with tasks and MERGE, and load files continuously with Snowpipe.
concepts.why: Pipelines that handle only what changed, built inside Snowflake, avoid reprocessing whole tables and need no outside scheduler.
concepts.body:
Three features combine into **pipelines**, chains of steps where each step's output feeds the next, that process only what changed.

**Streams** record changes (change data capture, CDC) to a table since the stream was last consumed: `CREATE STREAM orders_stream ON TABLE orders`. Selecting from a stream returns changed rows plus `METADATA$ACTION` (INSERT or DELETE), `METADATA$ISUPDATE` and `METADATA$ROW_ID`; an update appears as a DELETE plus INSERT pair. Reading a stream in a plain `SELECT` does not advance it. The offset moves only when the stream is used in a **DML statement that commits**. `APPEND_ONLY = TRUE` tracks inserts only and is cheaper. A stream that isn't consumed within the table's retention period becomes **stale**.

**Tasks** run SQL on a schedule (`SCHEDULE = '5 MINUTE'` or `'USING CRON 0 * * * * UTC'`) or after another task (`AFTER parent`), forming chains and trees of tasks. Leave out `WAREHOUSE` for a **serverless** task, which runs on compute Snowflake manages and bills for you. A `WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('s')` condition skips runs when there's nothing to do. Tasks are created **suspended**; run `ALTER TASK ... RESUME`.

**MERGE** applies the changes to a target, handling inserts, updates and deletes in one statement, the same idea as an upsert.

**Snowpipe** loads files automatically as they land in a stage, triggered by a notification from the cloud storage when a file arrives (`AUTO_INGEST = TRUE`) or by a request from your own program, using serverless compute. It runs a `COPY INTO` definition and keeps its own load history. **Snowpipe Streaming** writes rows directly from programs, such as connectors for the Kafka messaging system, with no files.
concepts.code:
CREATE STREAM orders_stream ON TABLE raw_orders;

CREATE TASK merge_orders
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
  SCHEDULE = '5 MINUTE'
  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('ORDERS_STREAM')
AS
MERGE INTO orders t
USING (SELECT * FROM orders_stream WHERE METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT') s
  ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.status = s.status, t.amount = s.amount
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (id, status, amount) VALUES (s.id, s.status, s.amount);

ALTER TASK merge_orders RESUME;          -- tasks start suspended

-- Continuous file ingestion from an external stage
CREATE PIPE orders_pipe AUTO_INGEST = TRUE AS
  COPY INTO raw_orders FROM @s3_orders_stage FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = JSON)
  MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME = CASE_INSENSITIVE;
takeaways: A stream's offset advances only when it's consumed by committed DML
Tasks are created suspended; WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA avoids empty runs
Snowpipe auto-ingests files; Snowpipe Streaming ingests rows
pitfalls: Forgetting ALTER TASK ... RESUME and wondering why nothing runs.

quiz.q: You SELECT * FROM a stream in a worksheet and then run the task. Does the task still see the changes?
options: Only if the stream is APPEND_ONLY
Yes, only committed DML that reads the stream advances its offset
quiz.explain: Plain queries don't move a stream's offset; DML using it in a committed transaction does.

quiz.q: How does a stream represent an UPDATE to a row?
options: As a DELETE and an INSERT with METADATA$ISUPDATE = TRUE
quiz.explain: Updates are represented as a DELETE/INSERT pair flagged with METADATA$ISUPDATE.

concepts.name: Dynamic tables
concepts.summary: Declare a pipeline as a query with a target lag and let Snowflake refresh it incrementally.
concepts.why: Dynamic tables replace much hand-written stream-and-task plumbing with one declarative statement.
concepts.body:
A **dynamic table** is defined by a query and a freshness goal. Snowflake keeps its contents up to date automatically:

```sql
CREATE DYNAMIC TABLE daily_revenue TARGET_LAG = '15 minutes' WAREHOUSE = etl_wh AS SELECT ...;
```

Key ideas:

- **TARGET_LAG** is how stale the table may be relative to its sources. Snowflake schedules refreshes to meet it. `TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM` means "refresh only as often as the dynamic tables that depend on me need".
- **Refresh mode**: with `REFRESH_MODE = AUTO` (the default) Snowflake uses **incremental** refresh, processing only changed source rows, when the query supports it, and a **full** refresh otherwise. You can set `INCREMENTAL` or `FULL` explicitly; check the chosen mode with `SHOW DYNAMIC TABLES`.
- Dynamic tables can read other dynamic tables, forming a pipeline that Snowflake refreshes step by step in the right order, each step seeing the same moment of the data.
- You can't `INSERT` or `UPDATE` them directly; the query is the only source of truth.

Compared with streams and tasks, dynamic tables suit transformations you can express as a single `SELECT` (joins, aggregations, flattening). Streams and tasks remain the tool for procedural logic, calling procedures, or exact control over when and how changes are applied.

Monitor refreshes with `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.DYNAMIC_TABLE_REFRESH_HISTORY()` or Snowsight's graph view, and suspend with `ALTER DYNAMIC TABLE ... SUSPEND` when you need to pause costs.
concepts.code:
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE order_lines
  TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
AS
SELECT e.src:id::INT AS order_id, i.value:sku::STRING AS sku, i.value:qty::INT AS qty
FROM raw_events e, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.src:items) i;

CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE sku_daily
  TARGET_LAG = '15 minutes'
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
AS
SELECT sku, SUM(qty) AS units
FROM order_lines
GROUP BY sku;

SHOW DYNAMIC TABLES LIKE 'SKU_DAILY';   -- check refresh_mode, target_lag, scheduling_state

ALTER DYNAMIC TABLE sku_daily REFRESH;  -- manual refresh when needed
takeaways: Define the result as a query plus a TARGET_LAG; Snowflake keeps it fresh
AUTO refresh mode picks incremental when the query allows it
Chain dynamic tables; use DOWNSTREAM lag for intermediate steps
pitfalls: Setting a very low TARGET_LAG on everything, which keeps warehouses busy and costs credits.

quiz.q: What does TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM mean for an intermediate dynamic table?
options: It copies the lag of its source table
It refreshes only when dynamic tables that depend on it need fresh data
quiz.explain: DOWNSTREAM defers scheduling to the consumers' lag targets.

concepts.name: UDFs, stored procedures and Snowpark
concepts.summary: Extend SQL with SQL and Python UDFs, write stored procedures, and use Snowpark DataFrames that run inside Snowflake.
concepts.why: Custom logic and Python data work can run next to the data instead of pulling it out.
concepts.body:
Snowflake runs code inside the platform in several forms.

- **SQL UDFs**: `CREATE FUNCTION f(x NUMBER) RETURNS NUMBER AS 'x * 2'`. Simple, fast, and often inlined into the query.
- **Python, Java, Scala and JavaScript UDFs**: the handler code runs in a locked-down area (a **sandbox**) on the warehouse. Python UDFs can use extra libraries (**packages**) from the built-in Anaconda channel via `PACKAGES = ('numpy')`. **Vectorized** Python UDFs receive whole groups of rows at once as pandas tables and are much faster than ones called row by row.
- **UDTFs** return a table, one input row producing many output rows.
- **Stored procedures** (SQL Scripting, Python, Java, JavaScript) run step-by-step logic and can execute SQL statements: repeating steps, creating tables, building SQL on the fly, catching errors. Call them with `CALL`. Procedures run with **owner's rights** by default or with `EXECUTE AS CALLER`.

**Snowpark** is a library for Python, Java and Scala that lets you build queries as chains of method calls on a **DataFrame**, a table-like object in your code. You write `session.table("orders").filter(col("amount") > 100).group_by("region").agg(...)`; nothing executes until an action such as `collect()` or `show()`, and then Snowpark turns the whole chain into SQL that runs on the warehouse. Data never leaves Snowflake unless you `to_pandas()` it. The same session can register UDFs from Python functions.

SQL Scripting blocks (`DECLARE ... BEGIN ... END`) can also run anonymously, without creating a procedure, which is handy for admin scripts.
concepts.code:
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION net_price(price NUMBER(10,2), vat NUMBER(4,2))
  RETURNS NUMBER(10,2)
  AS 'price / (1 + vat)';

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION slugify(s STRING)
  RETURNS STRING
  LANGUAGE PYTHON
  RUNTIME_VERSION = '3.11'
  HANDLER = 'slug'
AS $$
import re
def slug(s):
    return re.sub(r'[^a-z0-9]+', '-', s.lower()).strip('-')
$$;

SELECT net_price(121, 0.21), slugify('Hello, Snowflake World!');
-- 100.00 | hello-snowflake-world

-- Snowpark (Python), run from a client or notebook:
-- df = session.table("orders").filter(col("amount") > 100).group_by("region").count()
-- df.show()   # compiled to SQL and executed in Snowflake
takeaways: SQL UDFs for simple expressions; Python UDFs for richer logic
Vectorized Python UDFs receive groups of rows at once and are much faster
Snowpark DataFrames run nothing until an action, then become SQL that runs in Snowflake
pitfalls: Calling to_pandas() on a huge Snowpark DataFrame and pulling everything to the client.

quiz.q: When does a Snowpark DataFrame query actually execute?
options: When each method like filter() is called
When an action such as collect() or show() is called
quiz.explain: Transformations are lazy and are compiled to one SQL statement at action time.

concepts.name: Cost control and warehouse scaling
concepts.summary: Control spend with multi-cluster scaling policies, resource monitors, query acceleration and ACCOUNT_USAGE cost analysis.
concepts.why: Snowflake bills by consumption, so cost engineering is a core skill for anyone running it at scale.
concepts.body:
Cost in Snowflake is compute credits, storage and serverless features, which run on compute Snowflake manages (Snowpipe, clustering, tasks, search optimization). Compute usually dominates, so focus there.

**Multi-cluster warehouses** (Enterprise edition) add clusters when queries queue: `MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1, MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 4`. `SCALING_POLICY = STANDARD` starts clusters quickly to avoid queuing; `ECONOMY` waits until there's enough load to keep a new cluster busy, saving credits at the price of some queuing. Scale **up** (size) for slow individual queries, **out** (clusters) for concurrency.

**Resource monitors** cap credits per warehouse or account per period. They can notify at a threshold and suspend warehouses at the limit, either letting running queries finish or killing them immediately.

**Query Acceleration Service** hands parts of large scans to serverless compute for unusually big queries, without resizing the warehouse. **Statement timeouts** (`STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS`), time limits per query, stop runaway queries.

Measure, then act:

- `SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY` gives credits per warehouse per hour.
- `QUERY_HISTORY` (and `QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY` for per-query credits) finds the expensive patterns.
- `ACCOUNT_USAGE` views lag real time by up to a few hours.

Typical wins: right-size warehouses and auto-suspend, consolidate idle warehouses, fix queries that scan entire tables, use transient tables for reloadable data, and shorten Time Travel on churny staging tables.
concepts.code:
ALTER WAREHOUSE bi_wh SET
  MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1
  MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 4
  SCALING_POLICY = 'ECONOMY'
  STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS = 1800;

USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR bi_monthly WITH
  CREDIT_QUOTA = 500
  FREQUENCY = MONTHLY
  START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY
  TRIGGERS ON 80 PERCENT DO NOTIFY
           ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND;
ALTER WAREHOUSE bi_wh SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = bi_monthly;

-- Credits per warehouse over the last 30 days
SELECT warehouse_name, ROUND(SUM(credits_used), 1) AS credits
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY
WHERE start_time >= DATEADD(day, -30, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP BY warehouse_name
ORDER BY credits DESC;
takeaways: Scale up for slow queries, out (multi-cluster) for concurrency
Resource monitors notify and suspend at credit thresholds
Measure with ACCOUNT_USAGE metering and query history before tuning
pitfalls: Raising warehouse size to fix queuing, which doubles cost without adding concurrency.

quiz.q: What does SCALING_POLICY = 'ECONOMY' trade off?
options: Lower credits for possibly more queuing
Nothing; it is just a label
quiz.explain: Economy starts extra clusters only when they'd stay busy, saving credits but tolerating some queuing.

concepts.name: Search optimization and materialized views
concepts.summary: Speed up needle-in-a-haystack lookups with search optimization and repeated totals with materialized views, and know their costs.
concepts.why: Some workloads don't prune with clustering alone, and these services exist exactly for them.
concepts.body:
Clustering helps range filters on a few columns. Two Enterprise-edition services cover other patterns, each with background maintenance billed as serverless credits (compute Snowflake manages) plus extra storage.

**Search optimization** builds a saved lookup structure, a kind of index, so lookups that match very few rows can skip most micro-partitions:

- equality and `IN` filters on high-cardinality columns (find one customer's rows among billions),
- searches for text inside a value or by pattern (`ON SUBSTRING(col)`),
- lookups inside VARIANT values and on map (geospatial) values.

Enable it per column and kind of search: `ALTER TABLE t ADD SEARCH OPTIMIZATION ON EQUALITY(customer_id)`. It suits queries returning a few rows; it does little for large scans.

A **materialized view** stores a pre-computed query result that Snowflake keeps current in the background. Queries on the view are always consistent with the base table: if maintenance is behind, Snowflake combines the stored result with the newer base data. The optimizer can even rewrite queries against the base table to use a matching view. Limits: a materialized view queries a **single table** with no joins, and supports a restricted set of functions and aggregates.

Choose by pattern: repeated heavy aggregations on one table call for a materialized view; needle-in-haystack filters call for search optimization; multi-table transformations call for dynamic tables. Check the maintenance cost with `SEARCH_OPTIMIZATION_HISTORY` and `MATERIALIZED_VIEW_REFRESH_HISTORY` before keeping them.
concepts.code:
-- Point lookups on a high-cardinality column
ALTER TABLE events ADD SEARCH OPTIMIZATION ON EQUALITY(customer_id), SUBSTRING(url);
SHOW TABLES LIKE 'EVENTS';   -- search_optimization: ON, progress: 100 when built

SELECT * FROM events WHERE customer_id = 'c_8f2a91';   -- prunes most partitions

-- Pre-aggregate a heavy, repeated query on one table
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_event_counts AS
SELECT TO_DATE(event_ts) AS day, event_type, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM events
GROUP BY TO_DATE(event_ts), event_type;

-- Always consistent with events, even right after new inserts
SELECT * FROM daily_event_counts WHERE day = CURRENT_DATE();
takeaways: Search optimization accelerates selective equality, substring and VARIANT lookups
Materialized views keep single-table aggregates fresh and always consistent
Both add serverless maintenance and storage costs: measure them
pitfalls: Creating a materialized view on a table that changes constantly, where maintenance credits outweigh savings.

quiz.q: Analysts often search a 5-billion-row table for one order_id. Which feature fits best?
quiz.explain: Highly selective equality lookups on a high-cardinality column are search optimization's use case.

quiz.q: Which query can a Snowflake materialized view NOT be defined with?
options: A GROUP BY on one table
A projection of a few columns
quiz.explain: Materialized views are limited to a single table; use a dynamic table for joins.

concepts.name: Data governance and secure data sharing
concepts.summary: Protect columns with masking policies and rows with row access policies, and share live data with other accounts without copying it.
concepts.why: Regulated data needs fine-grained controls, and sharing without copies is one of Snowflake's defining features.
concepts.body:
Beyond grants, Snowflake offers policy objects (Enterprise edition) that are attached to columns and tables and evaluated at query time for every user.

**Masking policies** transform a column's value depending on context: `CREATE MASKING POLICY ... AS (val STRING) RETURNS STRING -> CASE WHEN IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('PII_READER') THEN val ELSE '***' END`. Attach one to any number of columns with `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN ... SET MASKING POLICY`. Prefer `IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION` over `CURRENT_ROLE()` so inherited and secondary roles count. **Tag-based masking** attaches a policy to a tag such as `pii = 'email'`, so every tagged column is protected automatically.

**Row access policies** return a boolean per row, typically by looking up the user's role in a mapping table, so one table can serve many regions or customers.

**Secure data sharing** grants other Snowflake accounts read access to live objects. The provider creates a **share**, grants database, schema and table or secure-view privileges to it, and adds consumer accounts. The consumer creates a read-only database from the share. No data is copied or moved: the consumer queries the provider's storage with the **consumer's own warehouse**, and sees updates immediately. Share subsets through **secure views**: shares accept secure objects by default, because an ordinary view's definition and optimizations could reveal data it is meant to hide. Sharing across regions and clouds relies on copying the data there (replication), which Marketplace listings can automate. Reader accounts let you share with organizations that don't have Snowflake.
takeaways: Masking policies change column values per role at query time
Row access policies filter rows per user or role
Shares give live, read-only access with no copies; consumers pay compute
pitfalls: Trying to share a plain view; create it as a SECURE VIEW so its definition and filtered rows stay protected.

quiz.q: Who pays for the compute when a consumer queries data from a share?
options: The consumer, using its own warehouse
quiz.explain: The consumer runs queries on its own warehouse; the provider pays only for storage.

quiz.q: Why prefer IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('PII_READER') over CURRENT_ROLE() = 'PII_READER' in a masking policy?
options: It also matches when PII_READER is inherited or active as a secondary role
quiz.explain: IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION respects the role hierarchy and secondary roles.
